questions.title: Leading a latency initiative without formal authority
questions.question: Tell me about a time you led a performance improvement effort without directly managing the engineers involved.
clarifyingQuestions: Was the primary problem average latency or tail latency?
Which teams controlled the largest parts of the critical path?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating whether the candidate uses data to align teams
answerOutline: Frame the business or trading impact
Explain how you created shared visibility
Describe the decisions you drove across teams
Quantify the latency and reliability outcome
questions.sampleAnswer: In one market-data distribution stack, p99 latency had crept up after several teams added safety checks and logging independently. I did not manage those teams, but I was asked to coordinate a fix before a known high-volume event because the issue crossed application, platform, and network boundaries. I started by building a single measurement view that broke the end-to-end path into components and showed each team exactly where the regression sat, which made the conversation fact-based instead of opinion-based. Then I proposed a two-week plan with small reversible changes, explicit owners, and a daily checkpoint so we could remove duplicate serialization, move one expensive metric off the hot path, and tighten CPU pinning without creating rollout risk. We reduced p99 latency by 37 percent, removed two sources of jitter, and went through the event without operational issues. What I learned is that senior leadership in this environment is often about making tradeoffs visible and giving busy peer teams a low-friction way to contribute, not about having direct reporting lines.

Focusing on heroics instead of how priorities and tradeoffs were managed
followUps: How did you handle resistance from a team that disagreed with your diagnosis?
What would you have done if the event date moved closer and you had even less time?
questions.seniorExtension: Explain how you would institutionalize the measurement and ownership model so the same regression pattern is caught automatically next time.

questions.sampleAnswer: I inherited a service that every release team depended on, but deployments were fragile because configuration, binaries, and rollback logic were all coupled together. Several peers felt a migration to immutable artifacts and automated rollback was too disruptive, so my job was to prove that the bigger risk was keeping a system nobody trusted. I broke the work into stages, starting with passive shadow validation and identical release metadata, so we could show parity before any user-facing cutover. I also published explicit go or no-go criteria, ran rehearsals with support teams, and kept a manual fallback for the first two releases so the organization could see we were being aggressive about improvement but conservative about exposure. After the cutover, failed deployments dropped sharply and mean recovery time on bad releases went from over half an hour to single digits. The key leadership move was translating a technical migration into an operational trust problem that everyone already felt, then giving them evidence that the transition was controlled.

I reframed the discussion around which capability truly had to be in the hot path for the first release and which parts could be staged behind feature flags and slower post-trade workflows. That allowed us to commit to a narrow first milestone with explicit operational guardrails, while a second milestone tackled the reliability items that would have made a broad launch dangerous. We met the business deadline, avoided a risky all-or-nothing release, and built more trust because both groups could see their concerns had been heard and translated into the plan. The lesson for me was that leadership often means sequencing disagreement into a roadmap instead of trying to win the argument in one meeting.

questions.title: Resolving a design disagreement on complexity versus simplicity
questions.question: Tell me about a time you strongly disagreed with another senior engineer on a design choice.
clarifyingQuestions: Was the disagreement about performance, reliability, or maintainability?
answerOutline: Describe the decision and relationship outcome
questions.sampleAnswer: I once disagreed with another senior engineer who wanted a lock-free queue everywhere in a pipeline where I thought a simpler bounded single-threaded stage would be safer and fast enough. The risk was that we were both optimizing for good goals, but continued argument without evidence would have burned time and strained the relationship. I suggested we write down the hypotheses we each believed, then benchmark two representative workloads and include failure-mode analysis such as backpressure and shutdown behavior rather than raw throughput alone. The results showed the lock-free version helped only one bursty path, while the simpler design gave cleaner operability for the broader service, so we used a hybrid design and kept the specialized queue only where it paid for itself. Because the decision came from shared criteria, not status, the relationship stayed strong and we kept working well together. That experience reinforced that senior disagreement should produce better decision quality, not silent resentment.

Ignoring the interpersonal side after the technical decision

questions.title: Diagnosing a memory leak causing latency regression
questions.question: Describe a production issue that was difficult to diagnose and how you worked through it.
clarifyingQuestions: Was the issue continuous or only under certain traffic shapes?
questions.sampleAnswer: I handled a case where tail latency degraded only after several hours of healthy operation, which made the issue easy to miss in short tests and hard to isolate during business hours. Rather than jumping between theories, I built a short hypothesis list around allocation growth, cache churn, and background compaction and assigned one observable to each. Heap profiles and allocation sampling eventually showed a small per-request object retained by an asynchronous callback path that rarely completed under one specific timeout mode. Once we fixed that path, I added long-duration soak tests and a production dashboard that paired latency with memory growth rate so similar slow-burn issues would surface earlier. The fix removed the leak and brought p99 back in line, but the bigger win was teaching the team to test for time-dependent failure modes instead of only peak load. In incident ownership, I try to leave behind a better detection model, not just a closed ticket.
commonMistakes: Listing tools without explaining the reasoning sequence
Skipping how you limited risk while diagnosis was ongoing

questions.title: Choosing the right ownership primitive in hot code
questions.question: How do you choose between raw pointers, std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, and std::weak_ptr in performance-sensitive C++ systems?

Confusing observing pointers with owning pointers

questions.title: ABA and memory reclamation in lock-free structures
questions.question: What is the ABA problem, and how would you address memory reclamation in a lock-free stack or queue?

questions.sampleAnswer: ABA happens when a compare-exchange sees the same pointer value twice and assumes nothing changed, even though the pointed-to node may have been removed, freed, and reused in between. A classic example is `head.compare_exchange_weak(old, old->next)` on a lock-free stack: if another thread pops `old`, frees it, and allocates a new node at the same address, the CAS can succeed on a logically invalid state. Tagged pointers can reduce the ABA risk by extending identity, but they do not solve reclamation by themselves; you still need a policy such as hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, or reference counting to ensure removed nodes are not freed while another thread may still observe them. In many low-latency systems I prefer epoch-based reclamation when thread sets are stable because it keeps the fast path simple, while hazard pointers give finer control at the cost of more per-access bookkeeping. The real senior answer is that lock-free correctness is never just about the CAS loop; reclamation strategy is part of the data structure definition.

questions.title: epoll edge-triggered versus level-triggered

questions.question: How would you design capacity planning and performance regression detection for a trading platform that experiences bursty market conditions?
clarifyingQuestions: Do you have realistic historical traffic captures for stressful periods?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating whether the candidate plans for tails and bursts instead of average load
answerOutline: Define capacity in terms of latency and correctness, not only throughput
Use historical burst replays and synthetic worst cases
Track headroom per stage and per resource domain
Feed findings back into rollout gates and hardware planning
Model venue or market-event specific stress patterns
questions.sampleAnswer: I define capacity as the point where the platform can still meet latency and correctness goals under stressful traffic, not merely the point where it has not crashed. To plan for that, I use historical captures from volatile sessions plus synthetic worst-case bursts so we understand queue growth, recovery behavior, and tail latency before the real market day arrives. Headroom needs to be tracked per stage and per resource domain—CPU, memory bandwidth, NIC queues, exchange throttles, and downstream consumers—because the first bottleneck is rarely the same across all conditions. I would automate regression detection against baseline runs so new code, new configs, or even new hardware microcode cannot drift into production unnoticed. Those results should feed rollout gates and hardware planning, otherwise load tests become ceremonial and disconnected from operational decisions. The strong design plans for burst behavior explicitly because that is where trading systems earn or lose trust.
